title: AI will hit an energy wall within three years, and the fix is to build a computer that isn't a computer
dek: Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.
why: The first half is the energy math; the second half is his first public reveal of a physical dynamics computer prototype and measured efficiency numbers, which is rare hard information. The biology analogy in the middle can be fast-forwarded.
who: Founders, investors and hardware engineers watching AI compute costs, data center power constraints and new chip architectures.
skip: 07:04 to 10:06, the biology and computer history analogies, low information density, skip to 12:07.

points.h: Energy isn't a cost line, it's the ticket to entry
points.body: Naveen's math: Google crosses 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, a low estimate, that's 12 gigawatts. The US today puts about 40 gigawatts into data centers; the world, under 100 gigawatts. So one company's AI service eats more than a tenth of global data center energy. His call is that we hit the energy ceiling in about three years. More important, the ranking of scarce resources in a data center has flipped: it used to be floor space, racks, networking gear, GPUs; today it's energy — get the power contract first, then figure out how to fill it. And energy is 50% of the cost of serving a token; the rest is hardware capex and site.

points.h: What a squirrel does on 8 milliwatts, a GPU needs watts for
points.body: A human brain is about 20 watts. Scale linearly by neuron count down to a monkey brain and you get one watt, exactly your phone in your pocket. Further down, mice and bats are milliwatt-scale. A squirrel leaping between branches, a thousand times out of a thousand, does it on an 8-milliwatt brain. So your phone's battery could run a hundred-plus squirrel brains. Naveen's conclusion is that biology has already built a physical substrate suited to intelligence, while synthetic systems took a different path: the human cortex moves only about 16 billion bits per second, a high-end GPU moves close to 30 trillion bits per second in and out of memory, and inside the chip it's another 10 to 100 times higher. The energy goes almost entirely into moving information, not computing on it.

points.h: Moore's Law stopped, and the abstraction layers still charge rent
points.body: Transistor counts are still rising, but frequency stopped scaling long ago, single-thread performance stopped, and now even efficiency no longer improves as process nodes shrink — Naveen flatly says Moore's Law is basically over. His diagnosis is the abstraction layers: digital itself is an abstraction of the physical world, transistors actually have intermediate states and are engineered into 0s and 1s. Every layer of abstraction is lossy and ignores the complexity beneath it. So their approach is to wire the physics of the semiconductor directly to the neural network, skipping the layers in between. His intuition pump is flocks of birds and ant colonies: individuals do something extremely simple, the whole emerges into complex behavior, and the field is called dynamical systems theory.

points.h: Metronomes on a board sync themselves up
points.body: Put several metronomes on a rigid board that can roll back and forth, and they synchronize to exactly the same phase on their own, just because each metronome gives the board a tiny push. That's a purely physical dynamical system. Their question was: can this kind of system compute? The answer is yes — they open-sourced an image generation model called UNO built on a set of such oscillators, and it trains and generates images. Define the system state as the phases of all the oscillators, condition on the output, and generating a plane, a car or a bird follows different state space trajectories. It's the first proof that this class of system can be trained at scale and produce useful results.

points.h: Throwing away connections makes the system easier to train
points.body: Fully connected is n squared: 10 elements, 100 connections, fine; 1,000 elements, a million connections, not scalable at all. Their sparsity is deliberately discarding some connections and seeing whether the overall behavior can be rescued. The result isn't just that you can throw them away — after throwing them away the system behaves better and is more trainable, and that holds in both simulation and real physical systems. Naveen says this is the rare case where more efficient, more scalable and better performing all hold at once, a holy grail nobody had cracked, provided you frame the problem correctly first.

points.h: The first physical dynamics computer has already generated images
points.body: This is Naveen's first public reveal: they built the first physical dynamics computer. The company only formally started in January of this year, with no team at the time; on June 1 they sent the design to tape-out, and the chip is back in the lab and has produced results — the first images generated by this kind of computer. On efficiency, generating an image takes about 500 nanojoules, versus millijoule scale for an ordinary GPU; a nanojoule is 10 to the minus 9, several orders of magnitude apart. The reason is that it doesn't move information at all. Architecturally it's unlike both CPUs and GPUs: those are von Neumann architectures, with memory and compute separated and data shuttled back and forth; in this machine compute and storage are the same thing, there is no memory interface, and every compute unit is itself a memory.

points.h: 4D computing: three spatial dimensions plus one of time
points.body: They call this 4D computing: physically, die stacking uses all three dimensions vertically and in-plane, and the fourth dimension is time in the dynamics. The objective function is intelligence per watt. There is a thermodynamic limit that can never be crossed; animal brains are only one to two orders of magnitude from it, while today's computing systems are about 10 billion times away. Their plan is to hit the limit of 2D lithography within three and a half years, and the company's overall goal is to beat biology. Naveen expects the result to be a change in form factor: from gigawatt-scale giant data centers to small data centers scattered everywhere, more local, more adaptive, and supporting billions of robots that dynamically combine to solve problems.

points.h: A thousand times cheaper means a thousand times more consumption
points.body: Naveen closes with the Jevons paradox: when the underlying cost of an asset falls, consumption grows by more than the price drop. Halve the price, consumption more than doubles; cut the price to a thousandth, consumption grows more than a thousandfold. So he doesn't think efficiency gains shrink the market — they create the largest market in human history. Chamath then presses on the ecosystem — tape-out, packaging and so on need a whole set of people to cooperate. Naveen's answer is a complete product within two years, in the form of a whole rack, as a new data center product, tokens in, tokens out over the network, but with an internal structure completely different from existing computers.

points.h: What ports over is the model layer, not the operator layer
points.body: Chamath asks whether existing model families and architectures can move over, given the whole industry is built around mechanisms like the KV cache. Naveen says there's a sliding scale: how much better something is determines how much migration pain people will tolerate, and his strategy is to make the gain from migrating large enough. The port happens at the model layer, not the operator layer; existing models work, but the migration itself takes considerable compute. He points out in particular that something like matmul doesn't exist on this machine — you can describe it as matrix multiplication, but it isn't implemented as matrix multiplication, it's implemented as behavior that changes over time, where each time step can be analyzed as the current state matrix times a transition matrix. On team composition, dynamical systems theory has existed for a hundred years, so they hire from that community, and they also hire people who actually build chips, and those two groups don't talk to each other, which makes coordination the hardest part of this company.

terms.def: A mathematical framework, about a hundred years old, for studying how simple individual rules give rise to complex collective behavior.
A computer structure in which memory and compute are separate and data is shuttled back and forth between them; CPUs and GPUs are both of this type.
Deliberately discarding some connections in a system, which instead makes the overall behavior better, more trainable and more scalable.
When the efficiency of using a resource improves, total consumption rises rather than falls.
Naveen's concept: use all three spatial dimensions physically, with the fourth dimension being time in the dynamics.
Defining the state as the phases of all the system's oscillators, and observing the path it traces as it evolves over time.
